references.text: Jesus calls his contemporaries "an evil generation" that demands signs. The parallel passage is found in [ref:Matt 12:39|Matthew 12:39], where Jesus says the same thing and points to the sign of Jonah as the only sign that will be given.
The following verse in [ref:Luk 11:30|Luke 11:30] explains how Jonah became a sign for the people of Nineveh, just as the Son of Man will be a sign for this generation.

In [ref:Matt 12:38-42|Matthew 12:38-42], we find the expanded parallel where the scribes and Pharisees ask for a sign, and Jesus responds by pointing to the sign of Jonah, the repentance of Nineveh, and the visit of the Queen of the South.

[ref:Matt 16:1-4|Matthew 16:1-4] describes another occasion where the Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign from heaven, and Jesus again calls them "an evil and adulterous generation" and refers to the sign of Jonah.
In [ref:Mark 8:11-12|Mark 8:11-12], the Pharisees ask for a sign from heaven, and Jesus sighs deeply and says that no sign will be given to this generation.

Jonah's three days and three nights in the belly of the fish ([ref:Jon 2:1|Jonah 2:1]) is the Old Testament basis for "the sign of Jonah" that Jesus refers to—a typological connection to Jesus' death and resurrection.
Jonah preached to Nineveh, and the people repented ([ref:Jon 3:4-5|Jonah 3:4-5]). Jesus uses the repentance of Nineveh as a contrast to the unbelief of his own generation.

The expression "this evil generation" is repeated in [ref:Matt 12:45|Matthew 12:45], where Jesus concludes the parable of the unclean spirit by saying that this will be the fate of this evil generation.
Paul writes in [ref:1 Kor 1:22|1 Corinthians 1:22] that the Jews demand signs, which reflects the attitude Jesus criticizes here.

In [ref:Joh 2:18-19|John 2:18-19], the Jews demand a sign from Jesus, and he responds by pointing to the destruction of the temple and its raising up in three days—a parallel to the sign of Jonah and the resurrection.
In [ref:Joh 6:30|John 6:30], the crowd again asks for a sign so that they may believe, showing the persistent demand for signs that Jesus encountered.
